source_text: Esse igitur hoc a Deo imperatum, quod asserimus, claruit; et quamvis sententiae ipsius aperta et intellectui omnium conciliata germanitas nullius in se naevum obscuritatis admiserit, tamen, ne tu ad ingenii nostri confugias tarditatem et dicas non nos intellegere quod praeceptum est, alio quoque testimonio non iam praecepti, sed operis secundum praeceptum exerciti, quemadmodum sit lex intellecta, doceamus. Legimus in libro quarto Regnorum de Amessia, filio Ioas, regis Iuda: Factum est, inquit, postquam stabilitum est regnum in manibus eius, occidit pueros suos, qui occiderant patrem suum; sed filios eorum non occidit secundum testamentum legis Domini, quo praeceptum est: Non morientur patres pro filiis nec filii pro patribus [n32] . Vides, quemadmodum historiae fides iustitiam regis iudicantis ostenderit, qui quamvis fuisset devotus, tamen, quoniam claudicasse animo in nonnullis refertur, ad iudicii eius confirmationem commemoratae legis Dei accessit auctoritas; ne enim parum haberet ponderis factum hoc consideratione facientis, secundum legem et testamentum Dei commendatur impletum.
pass_a_gloss: It has therefore become clear that this which we assert was commanded by God; and although the open kinship of the sentence itself, reconciled to the understanding of all, has admitted into itself no blemish of obscurity, nevertheless, lest you take refuge in the slowness of our talent and say we do not understand what was precepted, let us also by another testimony, not now of a precept but of a work exercised according to the precept, teach how the law was understood. We read in the fourth book of Kingdoms concerning Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah: It was done, he says, after the kingdom was established in his hands, he killed his boys who had killed his father; but he did not kill their sons according to the testament of the law of the Lord, by which it is precepted: Fathers shall not die for sons nor sons for fathers. You see how the faith of the history has shown the justice of the judging king, who although he had been devoted, nevertheless, since he is reported to have limped in mind in some things, the authority of the commemorated law of God acceded to the confirmation of his judgment; for lest this deed have too little weight by consideration of the doer, it is commended as fulfilled according to the law and testament of God.

lemmas.lexica: LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: It has therefore become clear that God commanded what we maintain. Although the plain, genuine meaning of the pronouncement itself is accessible to everyone’s understanding and contains no blemish of obscurity, you might still take refuge in accusing us of slow intelligence and say we do not understand the command. So let us use another testimony, this time not a command but an action performed according to the command, to show how the law was understood.

In the fourth Book of Kingdoms, we read about Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah: ‘After the kingdom was firmly established in his hands, he killed his servants who had killed his father. But he did not kill their sons, in accordance with the covenant of the Lord’s law, which commands: Fathers shall not die for their children, nor children for their fathers’ (2 Kings 14:5–6). You see how the truthful historical account displays the justice of the king’s judgment. Although he had been devout, he is reported to have faltered in some respects. The authority of God’s law was therefore recalled to confirm his judgment. So that the deed should not carry too little weight because of the person who did it, it is commended as having been performed according to God’s law and covenant.

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
